I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma of witnessing domestic violence, the trigger pattern is strongly male-linked ('being alone with men') but also includes 'being alone with women' without any corresponding formulation or symptom content explaining why both genders would be equivalently triggering. That broadens the trigger profile in a way that is hard to connect to the rest of the report, which is centered on interpersonal threat from others who might harm him rather than gender-nonspecific social presence.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Driving/being a passenger in a vehicle' is difficult to link to the reported trauma and the rest of the profile. No other trigger, threat, or memory item involves transport, accidents, escape, or vehicles, so this strategy appears to address a symptom domain not represented elsewhere in the five components.

vignette:
Rangi is an eighteen-year-old New Zealand-born Māori man who presents with a PCL-5 score of 55, seeking help for symptoms that have intensified markedly over the past several months. He is currently in a relationship and works as a junior project manager - a role that places him in daily contact with male colleagues, site supervisors, and contractors, a fact that has begun to corrode both his professional performance and his sense of safety at work.

Rangi grew up in a household where his father's drinking was the reliable prelude to violence. He remembers, with the particular clarity of a child who learned to read a room, how the smell of alcohol on his father's breath would arrive before the shouting did - how his father would wheel his bicycle up the front path after a night out, the creak of the gate and the scrape of tyres on concrete becoming sounds that meant something terrible was about to happen. He would watch from the hallway as his mother tried to manage the situation, and what he witnessed on those nights - the blows, the screaming, the way his mother's face changed - left impressions that did not organise themselves into a coherent story. He feels now that he only holds fragments of what happened: a hand raised, a particular quality of light, the texture of the carpet where he sat. The pieces do not fit together into something he can narrate from beginning to end, and the gaps feel as frightening as what he can recall, because he cannot be certain what is missing. When the memories do surface - triggered by a smell, a sound, a man standing too close - they do not feel like recollection. They carry the same terror he felt as a child, as though the event is still in progress.

The triggers that activate this response are specific and visceral. The smell of alcohol is perhaps the most immediate: when a colleague breathes near him after a lunchtime drink, or when a client opens a beer on a site visit, Rangi's body responds before his mind catches up. Being alone with men - in a meeting room, in a lift, on a quiet part of a construction site - produces a dread that he has come to regard as rational, because watching other people closely for signs of threat feels, to him, like the only sensible posture. He scans faces and postures constantly, reading micro-expressions for the shift his father's face used to make. Seeing a bicycle - even locked to a railing outside the office - can stop him mid-stride, pulling fragments of memory to the surface that arrive without context or sequence, incomplete and jagged.

These intrusions and the hypervigilance they sustain have shaped his behaviour in ways that have accumulated quietly into serious consequences. He has begun avoiding people wherever he can - eating lunch alone, declining after-work gatherings, routing his commute to avoid the bike rack near the entrance. At home he checks the doors and locks repeatedly before he can settle, sometimes three or four times in a single evening, and he startles violently at ordinary sounds: a door closing elsewhere in the building, a raised voice from a neighbouring apartment. The checking and the vigilance do not calm him; if anything, the act of scanning for danger keeps danger feeling imminent, and the hyperarousal that follows draws further fragments of memory to the surface, which in turn refreshes his certainty that the threat is real and present.

He drinks to manage this. He is aware, with a kind of grim irony he cannot fully articulate, that he is using the same substance that announced danger throughout his childhood. He smokes and, on worse nights, takes medication not prescribed to him. These strategies blunt the edge of the hypervigilance briefly, but they do not resolve it, and the morning after tends to bring a rawness - a lowered threshold - that makes the next trigger hit harder and the checking begin sooner.

What finally brought Rangi to seek help was a moment at work when a senior male colleague placed a hand on his shoulder and Rangi's response - freezing, then leaving the room without explanation - was witnessed by the team. He is most afraid that there is something permanently wrong with him, and most hoping, tentatively, that someone might be able to help him understand why the past keeps arriving in the present without warning.
